James Montgomery Boice
jaymz munt-GUM-er-ee boys
proper noun (figure)
James Montgomery Boice (1938-2000), American Reformed pastor and theologian. James (from Hebrew Jacob); Boice, an American surname. Usually styled "James Montgomery Boice."

Biblical Definition

James Montgomery Boice (1938-2000) was the American Reformed pastor, expositor, and broadcaster who pastored Tenth Presbyterian Church in Philadelphia for over thirty years and labored, through preaching, radio, and writing, for the recovery of Reformed, expository, gospel-centered ministry in late-20th-century evangelicalism. Educated at Harvard and at the University of Basel (where he studied under the shadow of European theology), Boice returned to pastor Tenth Presbyterian, one of the historic pulpits of American Presbyterianism, from 1968 until his death in 2000. His expository ministry produced massive commentary series — on Genesis, the Psalms, the Gospel of John, Romans, and the Minor Prophets — transcribed from his preaching. He was the longtime speaker on The Bible Study Hour radio broadcast and a founder and chairman of the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy, which produced the Chicago Statement (1978). Late in his life, alarmed by the drift of evangelicalism toward pragmatism, man-centered worship, and a diluted gospel, Boice helped found the Alliance of Confessing Evangelicals and was a principal author of the Cambridge Declaration (1996), which recalled the church to the five solas of the Reformation against the encroachments of the modern church-growth and seeker-sensitive movements. Diagnosed with aggressive cancer, Boice preached to his congregation about the sovereignty of God in his dying with a faith that moved many; he died weeks later, having written a final hymn. He stands as a model of the Reformed pastor-theologian: a faithful expositor of one pulpit for a generation, a defender of inerrancy and the solas, and a man whose dying magnified the God he had preached.

JAMES MONTGOMERY BOICE, proper noun. American Reformed pastor, expositor, and broadcaster (1938-2000).

Harvard- and Basel-educated; pastor of Tenth Presbyterian Church, Philadelphia, 1968-2000.

Massive expository commentary series (Genesis, Psalms, John, Romans, the Minor Prophets); speaker on The Bible Study Hour.

Founder and chairman of the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy (Chicago Statement, 1978).

Co-founder of the Alliance of Confessing Evangelicals; principal author of the Cambridge Declaration (1996), recalling the church to the five solas.

Romans 11:36 — "For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen."

2 Timothy 4:7-8 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness."

Psalm 115:1 — "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake."

Modern Corruption

James Montgomery Boice is corrupted when his decades of faithful expository ministry are forgotten behind flashier names, when the Cambridge Declaration's call to the solas is treated as mere nostalgia, or when his model of the settled pastor-theologian is despised in an age of celebrity and platform.

expand to see more

Settled-pastorate undervalued. Boice pastored one church for thirty-two years — the unglamorous, faithful, long obedience of expository ministry in a single pulpit. In an age that prizes platform, mobility, and the building of personal brands, the model of the settled pastor-theologian who pours his life into one congregation can seem small. It is not. Boice's massive commentary series, his radio ministry, and his confessional leadership all flowed from the faithful weekly exposition of Scripture to one people over decades. The dictionary honors the long obedience of the settled pulpit as the model it is.

Cambridge-Declaration-as-nostalgia misreading. The Cambridge Declaration (1996), which Boice helped author through the Alliance of Confessing Evangelicals, recalled evangelicalism to the five solas of the Reformation against the man-centered, pragmatic, market-driven church of the church-growth movement. Some hear this as backward-looking nostalgia for a Reformation long past. The dictionary hears it as a prophetic call: the solas — Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, to God's glory alone — are not period pieces but the permanent shape of the gospel, and Boice's generation needed the recall as much as Luther's needed the original. The drift the Declaration named (the church-growth-movement and seeker-sensitive entries develop it) has only deepened; the recall is more, not less, urgent.
